s01_title: This is v l a serve. It turns a trained robot policy into a local service, so a robot can use it with one command. In about four minutes, we will go from a checkpoint to a robot opening a drawer in simulation.
s02_problem: Deploying a vision language action model is harder than it looks. Every policy family has its own loading code, tokenizer, and normalization statistics. Library upgrades can break older checkpoints. Camera names and joint order must match the training data exactly. And the model needs a few hundred milliseconds, while the robot wants a new command every thirty three. v l a serve takes care of each of these.
s03_overview: There are two parts. On the GPU machine, a container loads the policy. On the robot, a small client of about eighty megabytes, with no PyTorch inside, sends camera frames, joint positions, and the instruction. It gets back the next fifty actions.
s04_build: Step one. Build the server image, once. It pins PyTorch, CUDA, and LeRobot to versions that work together. No model weights are inside. Checkpoints are mounted when you run it.
s05_inspect: Step two. Inspect the checkpoint. This reads only its metadata, so it is instant and needs no GPU. This SmolVLA policy expects two cameras, head and wrist, eight joint values, and a sentence. It returns fifty actions. Notice the source: the dataset statistics. After fine tuning, the config file can be out of date, so v l a serve trusts the statistics first.
s06_check: Step three. Check that the robot matches the policy. A robot profile names your cameras and joints. The K A A I R profile passes. The Lee-bear-oh profile fails, with three clear reasons. Mistakes like these are caught here, before anything moves.
s07_serve: Step four. Start the server. Mount your checkpoints read only, together with the Hugging Face cache, and pick a GPU. The model loads in about fifty seconds. Then health and p s confirm it is ready.
s08_ask: Step five. Ask for actions from Python. Before sending, the client resizes each frame to the network input, exactly as the policy itself would, and encodes it as JPEG. A request shrinks from two point four megabytes to under one hundred kilobytes, and the actions do not change. A missing camera is refused, with the reason.
s09_chunks: Because the policy returns a chunk of fifty actions, the robot never has to wait. The chunk executor plays one action every thirty three milliseconds, asks for the next chunk while the current one is still running, and drops the few actions that went stale while the model was thinking. In this run, there were zero stalls.
s10_sim: Step six. Run it. The served policy now drives the simulated K A A I R robot, in a room textured from photos of the real office. The task is: open the bottom drawer. A new chunk arrives every one point seven seconds, and the drawer opens twenty five centimeters in under ten seconds.
s11_results: How do we know that serving does not change the policy? First, for the same input and the same random seed, the served actions are identical to LeRobot's, bit for bit. Second, over fifty simulated episodes, the served policy succeeds as often as LeRobot running in process. Forty two out of fifty on the same device, and forty four with the default compression.
s12_end: Everything you saw is in the documentation, together with a short course on how VLAs work. Run make help to see every command. Thanks for watching.
